sections.title: Clinical Definitions & Overview
sections.content: The Trochlear Nerve (CN IV) innervates the Superior Oblique (SO) muscle, which depresses, abducts, and incyclotorts the eye. A palsy results in hypertropia and excyclotorsion. Conversely, Skew Deviation is a vertical misalignment caused by an imbalance in gravity-sensing vestibular pathways (otolith-ocular reflex), often mimicking a 4th nerve palsy but originating from brainstem or cerebellar pathology.

sections.title: Anatomical Path of CN IV
content: 1. Nucleus: Level of inferior colliculus in midbrain
2. Decussation: ALL fibers cross in the Superior Medullary Velum
3. Exit: Only CN to exit DORSALLY from the brainstem
4. Course: Longest intracranial course (7.5cm) around brainstem
5. Entry: Cavernous sinus (lateral wall) to Superior Orbital Fissure

sections.title: The Parks Three-Step Test (for CN IV)
content: Step 1: Identify which eye is higher (hypertropic) in primary gaze.
Step 2: Determine if the hypertropia increases on right or left gaze (Maximized when the affected SO is trying to act as a pure depressor).
Step 3: Determine if the hypertropia increases on right or left head tilt (Bielschowsky Head Tilt Test). Ipsilateral tilt increases hypertropia in 4th NP.

sections.title: Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR) Triad
content: Skew Deviation (Vertical misalignment)
Ocular Torsion (Incyclotorsion of the higher eye, excyclotorsion of the lower eye)
Head Tilt (Towards the side of the lower eye)

content.explanation: If the vertical deviation decreases by 50% or more when the patient moves from an upright to a supine (laying down) position, it is SKEW DEVIATION. CN IV palsies remain stable regardless of position.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Image Neuro?
content: Associated neurologic deficits (ataxia, weakness)
Papilledema or signs of increased ICP
Patient < 40 years old with no trauma history
History of malignancy
Positive Upright-Supine test result
Presence of Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR)

sections.title: Bilateral 4th NP Signs (The Traumatic Check)
content: 1. Reversal of hypertropia on side-to-side head tilt.
2. Excyclotorsion >10 degrees on Double Maddox Rod.
3. V-pattern Esotropia (narrower in upgaze).
4. Chin-down head position (compensating for lack of depression).
5. Fundus torsion visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Prism Cover Test: Primary, 8 cardinal gazes.
2. Parks 3-Step Test: Essential for verticality.
3. Double Maddox Rod: Quantify torsion (Subjective).
4. Fundus Photos: Quantify torsion (Objective).
5. Upright-Supine Test: Rule out Skew.
6. MRI Brain/Orbit: If neuro-signs or atypical.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Congenital 4th NP: Check old family photos for a head tilt ('FAT' scan: Family Album Tomography) and look for increased vertical fusion amplitudes (>3 prism diopters).
Ischemic CN IV: Typically recovers within 3-4 months. Watch and wait with a Fresnel prism.
Bilateral Surgery: Often requires Harada-Ito procedure for symptomatic excyclotorsion (moving the anterior SO tendon laterally).
Differential: Don't forget Myasthenia Gravis and Thyroid Eye Disease for any vertical diplopia!

content.explanation: Superiors are IN-torters (Superior Oblique and Superior Rectus). Superior Oblique is the primary in-torter.

sections.title: Landmark Study: Wong et al. (2011)
sections.content: The Upright-Supine test was validated as highly sensitive and specific for differentiating skew deviation from CN IV palsy. A reduction of vertical deviation by >50% in the supine position had 92% sensitivity and 100% specificity for Skew Deviation in their cohort.
